title: War on Drugs History: How It Shaped Cannabis Laws
h1: How the War on Drugs Shaped Cannabis Laws, From 1971 to Legalization
metaDescription: War on drugs history for cannabis: the 1971 launch, 1980s mandatory minimums, arrest numbers and costs, and how legalization is unwinding it as of 2026.
excerpt: A short timeline of the War on Drugs as it hit cannabis: the 1971 launch, the 1980s crackdown, who bore the cost and where things stand in October 2026.

body:
Any war on drugs history that involves cannabis starts in 1971, when President Nixon named drug abuse the nation's top enemy. Over the next five decades, enforcement grew, marijuana arrests climbed into the hundreds of thousands a year and the burden fell unevenly. State legalization, including Michigan's, has started to unwind that history, while federal law moves more slowly. Here's the short version.

## War on drugs history: 1971 and "public enemy number one"

On June 17, 1971, President Nixon told reporters that "America's public enemy number one in the United States is drug abuse." He called for "a new, all-out offensive," asked Congress for $155 million in new funds and named a White House special consultant to coordinate the effort.

The groundwork was already in place. The Controlled Substances Act, signed in 1970, had put marijuana in Schedule I, the strictest federal category. Our guide to the [Controlled Substances Act](/blog/controlled-substances-act-cannabis/) explains how that happened.

## Enforcement ramps up: a new federal agency, the 1980s and mandatory minimums

In 1973, a federal reorganization created the Drug Enforcement Administration, combining earlier drug agencies into one. The 1980s raised the stakes. The Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986 built the basic framework of federal mandatory minimum sentences, tying prison time to the type and amount of drug involved.

Under federal law today, trafficking cases involving 100 kilograms or more of marijuana carry a minimum of five years in prison, and 1,000 kilograms or more carry at least ten.

## Cannabis arrests by the numbers

| Period | Marijuana arrests | Reported by |
|---|---|---|
| 2001 to 2010 | More than 8 million in total | ACLU |
| 2018 | Almost 700,000, over 43% of all drug arrests | ACLU |
| 2024 | At least 204,036, about 92% for possession | FBI data compiled by NORML |

Recent counts are hard to compare with older ones because the FBI changed how it collects crime data in 2021, and some agencies don't report. Still, the totals have fallen as more states legalized.

## Who bore the burden: racial disparities in enforcement

The ACLU found that in 2018 a Black person was 3.64 times more likely than a white person to be arrested for marijuana possession, up from 3.31 times in 2010. That held even though Black and white Americans use marijuana at similar rates. This gap sits at the center of our look at [Black History Month and cannabis](/blog/celebrating-black-history-month/).

## What it cost: dollars, records and families

In 2013, the ACLU estimated that enforcing marijuana laws cost about $3.6 billion a year. The costs didn't stop at budgets. A conviction can show up in background checks for jobs and housing for years, and jail time, fines and court dates pull parents away from work and family.

Those lasting effects are why equity programs and record-clearing are now part of legalization. Our explainer on [cannabis social equity](/blog/cannabis-social-equity/) covers how states, Michigan included, approach it.

## The turn: medical laws, state legalization and Michigan's 2018 vote

States began changing course in the 1990s with medical cannabis laws. Michigan voters approved medical marijuana in 2008 and adult-use legalization in 2018, and the adult-use law took effect on December 6, 2018. Today adults 21 and older can buy from licensed stores, and registered patients 18 and older can too. Our [Michigan cannabis laws guide](/cannabis-laws-by-state/michigan/) covers the limits.

## Clearing old records in Michigan

Legal sales going forward don't erase old convictions on their own. Whether an old marijuana conviction qualifies depends on the offense and the rest of the record, so start with our guide to [Michigan marijuana expungement](/blog/michigan-marijuana-expungement/), which covers the process and where to find free help.

## Where federal policy stands now

As of October 2026, the federal fight over marijuana isn't finished. A final federal order effective April 28, 2026, moved marijuana covered by a state medical license, and marijuana drugs approved by the FDA, to Schedule III. All other marijuana, including adult-use, remains in Schedule I.

A broader proposal to move all marijuana to Schedule III went before a DEA administrative law judge this summer, and as of late October 2026 the recommended decision was still pending. Our [rescheduling explainer](/blog/cannabis-rescheduling/) tracks the latest. Until federal law changes, the old lines still matter, so don't travel across state lines with cannabis.

faq.q: When did the War on Drugs start?
faq.a: Many histories date it to June 17, 1971, when President Nixon called drug abuse "public enemy number one" and asked Congress for more money to fight it. The Controlled Substances Act, signed in 1970, had already placed marijuana in Schedule I, and the Drug Enforcement Administration followed in 1973.

faq.q: How many people are arrested for marijuana each year?
faq.a: Far fewer than at the peak, but still many. The ACLU counted almost 700,000 marijuana arrests in 2018. FBI figures compiled by NORML show at least 204,036 in 2024, about 92% of them for possession. Changes in how the FBI collects data since 2021 make year-to-year comparisons tricky, and some agencies don't report.

faq.q: Did the War on Drugs target certain communities?
faq.a: Enforcement fell unevenly. The ACLU found that in 2018, Black Americans were 3.64 times more likely than white Americans to be arrested for marijuana possession. That gap held even though both groups use marijuana at similar rates. Those records still affect jobs, housing and families, which is why record-clearing matters.

faq.q: Is the War on Drugs over?
faq.a: Not at the federal level. As of October 2026, adult-use marijuana is still a Schedule I controlled substance, though marijuana under a state medical license moved to Schedule III in April 2026. Michigan and many other states allow legal sales, but federal law still applies across state lines and on federal land.

claims.claim: On June 17, 1971, President Nixon said "America's public enemy number one in the United States is drug abuse."
claims.evidence: Remarks dated June 17, 1971, with the quoted sentence verbatim.

claims.claim: He called for "a new, all-out offensive," asked Congress for $155 million in new funds and named a White House special consultant.
claims.evidence: "it is necessary to wage a new, all-out offensive"; "I am asking the Congress for $155 million in new funds"; "appointment of Dr. Jerome H. Jaffe as Special Consultant to the President for Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs was released June 17, 1971".

claims.claim: The Controlled Substances Act, signed in 1970, put marijuana in Schedule I.
claims.evidence: "When Congress enacted the CSA in 1970, it placed marijuana in schedule I."

claims.claim: In 1973 a federal reorganization created the DEA, combining earlier drug agencies into one.
claims.evidence: Reorganization Plan No. 2 of 1973, "Eff. July 1, 1973": "There is established in the Department of Justice an agency which shall be known as the Drug Enforcement Administration"; the Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs "is hereby abolished"; message: "consolidation of our anti-drug forces under a single unified command". (dea.gov returned 403.)

claims.claim: The Anti-Drug Abuse Act of 1986 built the framework of federal mandatory minimums tied to drug type and amount.
claims.evidence: "created the basic framework of mandatory minimum penalties currently applicable to federal drug trafficking offenses ... based on the type and amount of drug mixture".

claims.claim: Federal trafficking cases with 100 kg or more of marijuana carry at least five years; 1,000 kg or more carry at least ten.
claims.evidence: 21 U.S.C. 841(b)(1)(A)(vii): "1000 kilograms or more ... marihuana, or 1,000 or more marihuana plants" - "not be less than 10 years"; (b)(1)(B)(vii): "100 kilograms or more ... or 100 or more marihuana plants" - "not be less than 5 years". In-text only (sources list at the 6 cap).

claims.evidence: "Between 2001 and 2010, there were over 8 million pot arrests in the U.S."

claims.evidence: "In 2018 alone, there were almost 700,000 marijuana arrests, which accounted for more than 43 percent of all drug arrests."

claims.evidence: "The FBI changed the way they collected and reported crime data in 2021 making it difficult to compare more recent datasets"; "some law enforcement agencies fail to report their arrest data to the FBI".

claims.claim: Totals have fallen as more states legalized; far fewer arrests than at the peak (FAQ).
claims.evidence: "2024's marijuana arrest totals are lower than in prior years and they continue a trend that began nearly a decade ago when state governments initially began regulating adult-use marijuana markets"; earlier peak of "over 870,000 marijuana-related arrests".

claims.claim: ACLU: "from 2010 to 2018, a Black person was on average 3.64 times more likely" to be arrested for possession (body and FAQ).
claims.fix: 3.64 is the 2018 rate ratio (2010 was 3.31). Body now says "in 2018 ... 3.64 times ... up from 3.31 times in 2010"; FAQ says "in 2018". The takeaway already tied 3.64 to 2018.
claims.evidence: Report Table 6 (2010-2018): 2010 ratio 3.31, 2018 ratio 3.64; "in 2018, they were 3.64 times more likely -- the greatest disparity of the past nine years".

claims.claim: The disparity held even though Black and white Americans use marijuana at similar rates.
claims.evidence: "even though Black and white people use marijuana at similar rates".

claims.claim: In 2013 the ACLU estimated marijuana enforcement cost about $3.6 billion a year.
claims.evidence: June 3, 2013: "Enforcing marijuana laws costs us about $3.6 billion a year".

claims.claim: States began changing course in the 1990s with medical cannabis laws.
claims.evidence: "California's 1996 medical-marijuana law, Proposition 215".

claims.claim: Michigan voters approved medical marijuana in 2008 and adult use in 2018; the adult-use law took effect December 6, 2018; adults 21+ and registered patients 18+ can buy.
claims.evidence: MMMA approved Nov. 4, 2008; MRTMA "effective Dec. 6, 2018"; adults 18+ register as patients.

claims.fix: No Michigan set-aside or expungement claim exists in facts/law-facts.json, and the rules say to leave such facts out and point readers on. Sentence removed; heading now "Clearing old records in Michigan". The section still sends readers to the Michigan expungement guide.
